summary: This informational RFC discusses long-term reporting of IP network performance metrics, over hours to months, for two audiences with different needs, and how those audiences affect the metric parameters chosen.

eli5.summary: Different people want different kinds of speed report: a driver wants today's traffic and a city planner wants a year. This explains how to report for each.

questions: how to report ip network performance metrics
who are the audiences for performance metrics
how long should a packet loss waiting time be
should lost packets have infinite delay
subtitle: How to report IP loss, delay and capacity measurements so they suit both network operators and application designers.

tldr.problem: The same IP performance measurements get used for different purposes, such as troubleshooting a network or predicting how an application will behave. Measurement settings and report formats that suit one audience can mislead the other.
tldr.mechanism: The memo separates two points of view, network characterization and application performance estimation, and shows how each affects loss, delay and capacity metrics. It recommends settings, such as a long loss waiting time and undefined delay for lost packets, that serve both audiences.
tldr.outcome: It is informational guidance for long-term reporting (hours to months) rather than a protocol. Its main advice is to measure once with generous settings and post-process for each audience.

today: RFC 6703 is an Informational document and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is guidance on reporting, not a protocol, and it refers to temporal aggregation details that it says were yet to be written.

sections.title: Two Audiences, Two Points of View
sections.content:
RFC 6703 starts from one question: how will the results be used? It names two audience categories, each with its own point of view (POV).

  • Network characterization describes conditions inside a network for quality assurance, troubleshooting, modeling and Service Level Agreements. It looks inward, toward the network where the report consumer intends to act.
  • Application performance estimation describes network conditions in a way that helps predict effects on user applications. It looks outward, toward the users, and accepts the network as it is. These are still IP-layer metrics, not application metrics.

The memo covers the loss and delay metrics ( RFC 2680, RFC 2679), touches on delay variation and reordering, and also covers capacity metrics. It builds on the IP Performance Metrics framework in RFC 2330 and focuses on "long-term" reporting: hours, days, weeks or months rather than 10 seconds.
sections.eli5: Some people want to fix the road and some people want to know how long their drive will take. They need different reports from the same measurements.

sections.title: Long-Term Reporting
sections.content:
Measurement intervals and reporting intervals need not be the same length. Running one measurement for weeks without saving intermediate results is risky: a power failure can lose everything, timing synchronization can fail and spoil a subset of results, and the measurement system may need maintenance. So the memo values measuring in intervals much shorter than the reporting interval.

It lists three ways to combine short intervals into a long-term statement: store every singleton result, use temporal aggregation as described in RFC 5835 (the memo says the details are yet to be written), or compare each interval with a numerical objective and report "metric A was at or below objective X during Y% of the time". Numerical thresholds of acceptability are not set in IETF performance work, so they are out of scope.

It also recommends limiting long-term loss and delay reports to intervals where connectivity can be demonstrated, and summarizing the rest as the percent of time where connectivity does not appear to exist. The minimal report must include both loss and delay.
sections.eli5: Instead of timing one huge race, you time lots of short laps and add them up. If a lap is ruined, you only lose that lap.

sections.title: Loss: How Long to Wait
sections.content:
A packet counts as lost if it does not arrive within a waiting time. RFC 2680 deliberately gives no value. Network characterization prefers a long wait, because routing loops during IGP re-convergence can delay packets by several seconds, and a long wait separates those late packets from ones dropped at a full queue.

The memo models a worst case with a loop: with 100 ms for every link and queue, TTL of 255, 5 queues on the path and 4 queues in the loop, the normal path delay is 1.1 seconds, the time in the loop is about 50 seconds, and the total is about 51.1 seconds. It says the figure is an upper limit for almost any real-world circumstance, and that a wait of approximately 50 seconds is manageable in practice.

Application designers usually care about shorter thresholds, but that is not a problem. A shorter threshold can be applied afterwards by re-designating packets that took longer as lost, so one long waiting time serves both audiences. The memo also recommends distinguishing lost packets from errored packets that did arrive ("conditionally lost"), which helps network characterization.
sections.eli5: How long do you wait for a friend before deciding they are not coming? Wait a long time, write down when they arrive, and later you can decide a shorter wait for each purpose.

sections.title: Delay and Lost Packets
sections.content:
The delay metric of RFC 2679 leaves the delay of a lost packet undefined, though informally it is sometimes called infinite. The memo argues for keeping it undefined and reporting delay as a distribution conditional on arrival.

  • Applications handle arriving and missing packets in two different ways (de-jitter buffer versus retransmission, concealment or forward error correction), so the difference must be preserved.
  • Loss and delay stay orthogonal: assigning infinite delay to lost packets would count them twice and make the delay CDF show a mass at infinity.
  • Delay variation in RFC 3393 already excludes lost packets, and assigning infinite delay would make the reordering metric of RFC 4737 treat them as reordered.

For statistics, the memo recommends reporting both the mean and the median of the conditional distribution. The median is stable against outliers but slow to show change, and both struggle with bimodal distributions, so the minimum, maximum and 95th percentile add value. For delay variation, use the minimum delay as the reference, and a useful report is a high percentile minus the minimum, for example the 99.9th percentile.
sections.eli5: If a letter never arrives, you do not say it took forever. You say it was lost, and you time only the letters that came.

sections.title: Reporting Capacity Metrics
sections.content:
Capacity comes in two kinds. Raw capacity ( RFC 5136) counts all IP-layer bits without regard to data uniqueness or congestion response. Restricted capacity ( RFC 3148) is Bulk Transfer Capacity (BTC), unique payload bits per elapsed time over a congestion-aware connection. The memo notes the obvious pairing of raw with network characterization and restricted with applications is too simple.

For raw capacity, IP-layer capacity, utilization and available capacity form a triad: knowing two determines the third. A commonly used utilization interval is 5 minutes, which hides a lot of variability; intervals near the serialization time of one MTU packet just show 100% or 0%. Reports of available capacity should name the method, the IP packet length, the maximum capacity the setup can assess, and the duration.

For BTC, the memo introduces a Type-C parameter describing TCP options and congestion control settings, and notes that measurements may include or exclude the 3-way handshake and slow start. A BTC report should name the method, MTU, maximum assessable BTC, time and duration, number of connections, and the congestion control algorithm.

To report variability, it suggests the minimum, maximum and range, the max/min ratio, moving averages, and often best of all a plot of singleton values over time.
sections.eli5: How much water can a pipe carry, how much is flowing, and how much room is left? Check at many times, because the answer keeps changing, and draw a picture.

sections.title: Test Streams, Sample Size and Security
sections.content:
Reports should describe the test stream and the sample size. Network characterization has traditionally used Poisson-distributed spacing for an unbiased sample, while application estimates often benefit from a stream resembling the application, such as a Periodic stream for real-time applications. For sample size, the memo says to state what the sample is meant to achieve rather than just call it large. It cites RFC 2330, where a sample of 128 singletons worked well for goodness-of-fit testing and 8192 almost always failed.

On security, the considerations for any active measurement of live networks apply; see RFC 4656. Long-term measurement leaves ports open longer and makes the activity easier to detect, and long waiting times give an attacker more opportunity to prepare a replay attack.
sections.eli5: Say how many times you checked, because more checks mean you can trust the answer more. And remember a long watch gives sneaky people more time to watch you back.
